sections.html:
Match the method to your deadline. East Windsor owners can work with an agent, go it alone, or take a cash offer, and the best fit depends on condition, tenants and timing. The township adds a step of its own: a fire prevention check of smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and an extinguisher before a single-family home or condominium is sold.

  • Working with an agent: reaches financed buyers, and takes the longest.
  • Going it alone: you handle price, contract and the township check yourself.
  • Cash sale as-is: helps with postponed repairs, a vacant property, or a hard deadline.

The Bureau of Fire Prevention checks smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and the fire extinguisher before a sale. Start by completing the Fire Inspection Form, then deliver or mail it with a $50 check or money order payable to East Windsor Township. Cards are refused, and the township asks for a week to process. A call follows to set the inspection, held mornings on varying days.

The resulting certificate lasts 60 days, so fix a closing date before booking. The inspector reviews how well the detectors work and how old they are, the extinguisher, the record of work and site conditions. Smoke detectors may be no older than 10 years and carbon monoxide detectors no older than 7, going by the manufacturer's label. A 2A10BC extinguisher with this year's tag must be in the kitchen, though it need not be mounted. Do not count on the inspector coming back quickly after a failure. Failing means repeating the process and paying a $25 re-inspection fee.

The township answers at 609-443-4000, extension 406, from the Municipal Building at 16 Lanning Boulevard.

sections.h2: Does East Windsor require a Certificate of Occupancy at resale?
sections.html:
The township's Certificate of Occupancy page names three residential triggers: new construction, additions, and reconstruction after fire, storm or vehicle damage. A plain resale is not one of them. The Construction Department also issues continued certificates and certificates of approval, so ask whether anything applies to your property, particularly if a reconstruction job never received a final sign-off.

For a rented house, owners are sent to the East Windsor Health Department at extension 416 for lead-based paint inspections in rental dwellings.

East Windsor has an estimated 30,562 residents, up from 30,045 in 2020. Owners live in about 61 percent of homes, and tenants in the rest. The middle owned home is valued at $397,400, and median household income is $105,208.

In Mercer County, East Windsor covers 15.57 square miles where the Delaware Valley meets the Raritan Valley, and it borders Robbinsville, West Windsor, Cranbury, Monroe, Plainsboro, Millstone and Upper Freehold. The independent borough of Hightstown sits wholly inside East Windsor. Twin Rivers, home to 7,878 people in 2020, was described in a state guide as New Jersey's first planned unit development. If your home is in Twin Rivers, ask the community association what paperwork it expects at resale.

Turnpike Exit 8 is inside the township and feeds Route 33 and Route 133, the Hightstown Bypass. U.S. Route 130 crosses the western part, with county routes 535 and 539 adding local links. Suburban Transit's 300 line goes to Port Authority in Midtown and its 600 line to Wall Street. The nearest NJ Transit rail stop is Princeton Junction, with a rush-hour shuttle, and Mercer County runs a shuttle along Route 130. The average commute is 26.8 minutes. Penn Medicine Princeton Medical Center is about 7 miles away in Plainsboro, which buyers sometimes ask about.

One district, East Windsor Regional School District, serves East Windsor and Hightstown. Name the school for your street in the listing, since buyers with children ask early.

sections.h2: What an East Windsor seller pays and where the deed goes
sections.html:
The state realty transfer fee is the seller's. The Mercer County Clerk's page adds that the graduated charge on sales of $1 million and up, starting at 1 percent, moved to the seller as of July 10, 2025.

  • Township check: $50 with the Fire Inspection Form, plus $25 if a second visit is needed.
  • Filing the deed: the Mercer County Clerk charges $43 for a regular deed's first page and $10 for every added page.
  • How to pay: transfer fees go in by cash, cashier's check, money order, attorney trust account or business escrow account, with certified or bank checks required above $10,000.
  • State form: a GIT/REP seller certification accompanies the deed.

The Records Room welcomes the public on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30, and the Indexing Section's number is 609-989-6476.

For a fast East Windsor sale, work backward from the date you want to close. Fix the closing date first, because the township certificate lasts only 60 days. Mail or drop off the Fire Inspection Form with the $50 payment about a week and a half ahead so the township has its week to process and the inspection can be scheduled. Replace any smoke detector older than 10 years, any carbon monoxide detector older than 7, and put a 2A10BC extinguisher with a current tag in the kitchen, so you pass the first time and skip the $25 re-inspection.

In parallel, ask your attorney or title agent to prepare the deed and the GIT/REP certification, and ask the Construction Department whether a past rebuild or addition needs a final certificate. Cash buyers can close as soon as these items are finished, while a mortgage buyer adds an appraisal and lender timeline on top.

If tenants live in the house, tell them about the inspection date in advance, since the inspector needs access to the kitchen and to each level with detectors. A vacant house is simpler to schedule, which is one reason owners of empty inherited properties often prefer a cash sale. Keep the receipt for the $50 payment and the certificate itself in the same folder as your closing documents, because the buyer's attorney will usually ask to see both. If the closing slips past 60 days from the inspection, plan on repeating the process, so it is better to book the inspection late than early.

faqs.q: Is a fire inspection required to sell in East Windsor?
faqs.a: Yes for a single-family home or condominium. The Bureau of Fire Prevention certifies detectors and an extinguisher before the sale, at $50, with a certificate good for 60 days.

faqs.q: What detector ages does East Windsor accept?
faqs.a: Smoke detectors up to 10 years old and carbon monoxide detectors up to 7, going by the manufacturer's label. The kitchen also needs a 2A10BC extinguisher with a current-year tag.

faqs.q: What if the East Windsor inspector fails my house?
faqs.a: Fix the items and run the process again with a $25 re-inspection fee. The certificate expires after 60 days, so book early enough to leave room for a second visit.

faqs.q: Will a resale in East Windsor require a Certificate of Occupancy?
faqs.a: The township's residential list covers new construction, additions and reconstruction. If your house was rebuilt after a fire or storm, ask Code Enforcement whether a final certificate was issued.

faqs.q: Who files an East Windsor deed?
faqs.a: The Mercer County Clerk. A regular deed runs $43 for page one and $10 for each page after, and the transfer fee has to arrive by an accepted method such as cash, cashier's check, money order or attorney trust account.
